offences.quote: Presenting another person’s work or ideas as your own without proper acknowledgement.
Presenting another person’s work or ideas as your own without proper acknowledgement.
Re-using your own work (wholly or in part) that has been submitted for a different assessment for which credit has been/is due to be awarded.
Assisting or enabling another person to engage in misconduct such as providing them with assessment material (paid or unpaid)
Obtaining assessment work created by a third party, whether paid or unpaid.
Inventing data, evidence, sources, references, or results.
Completing an assessment for another person or allowing this to occur.
Using materials, resources, or devices not permitted under assessment conditions.
Failure to comply with stated assessment requirements e.g. breaching exam or coursework rules or conditions.

liability.quote: The University applies a principle of ‘strict liability’ to breaches of academic integrity, this means that the student’s intentions are not relevant to determining whether or not a breach has occurred.
we do consider a student’s intentions when deciding on an appropriate outcome once a breach has been proven.

In cases where the assessed work is found to display poor levels of scholarship, and it is deemed appropriate to deal with this without formally recording an academic integrity breach, the Module Leader will ensure the mark reflects the poor scholarship and that the student is offered advice and support.

detection.quote: An Academic Integrity Adviser can request that a subject-matter expert attend the meeting to explore the student’s level of knowledge and understanding of the assessment topic.
detection.anchor: Meeting with an Academic Integrity Adviser (Level 2)

detection.quote: The University may use software and detection tools to support academic judgement investigations of academic integrity.
detection.anchor: Breaches of the policy and outcomes from investigations

process.quote: If the Module Leader supports the allegation, they should refer the case to the relevant Academic Integrity Adviser.
The University is committed to upholding the standards of academic integrity and will investigate any suspected breach of this policy.
process.anchor: Breaches of the policy and outcomes from investigations

process.quote: The student will be invited to meet with the Academic Integrity Adviser
Panel meetings can be online or face to face and may be recorded.
but if the student declines a second invitation then it will proceed without their attendance.
The student may be accompanied by a friend or adviser from the Students’ Union Advice Centre; however, they will not be able to speak on the student’s behalf.
process.anchor: Meeting with an Academic Integrity Adviser (Level 2)

process.quote: Students must appeal the outcome of an investigation within ten working days by contacting studentcasework@uwe.ac.uk
The student will be invited to meet with the Academic Integrity Adviser and will have five working days to confirm whether they will be attending.
the standard of proof that is used in this policy is the ‘balance of probabilities.’
Monitor breaches of academic integrity on an annual basis and use this data to inform academic practice.

formal penalties including mark reductions or failure of the assessment or module.

Mark of 0 for the work item, and mark reduction applied to the whole module (40% levels 3-6, 50% level 7) if a resit or retake is required.
In the most severe cases, students may be expelled from the institution entirely.

If upheld, this could potentially result in an award being revoked.

Outcomes of academic integrity breaches for students on awards validated or accredited by professional or statutory bodies may be constrained by the regulations of those bodies. This may include reporting the breach to the professional or statutory body.

definitions.quote: Presenting another person’s work or ideas as your own without proper acknowledgement.
Re-using your own work (wholly or in part) that has been submitted for a different assessment for which credit has been/is due to be awarded.
Unauthorised collaboration on work required to be completed individually.
Obtaining assessment work created by a third party, whether paid or unpaid.
Inventing data, evidence, sources, references, or results.
Deliberately altering data, evidence, or results.
Completing an assessment for another person or allowing this to occur.
Providing false or misleading information about your work or contribution.
the University does not consider whether the breach was an accident or was deliberate in concluding whether or not a breach has occurred
